A company runs a reporting application on a single Amazon EC2 instance that stores its data on an Amazon EBS gp3 volume. The application can tolerate up to 4 hours of data loss and up to 8 hours of downtime. If the instance's Availability Zone fails, the company must be able to recover the application in another Availability Zone in the same Region.

Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Use Data Lifecycle Manager to snapshot the volume every 4 hours. Restore the latest snapshot in another Availability Zone if needed.
options.note: EBS snapshots are stored regionally, so they can be restored to a volume in any Availability Zone in the Region. Snapshots every 4 hours meet the RPO, and a restore fits within the 8-hour RTO.

options.text: Enable EBS Multi-Attach on the volume and attach it to a stopped standby instance in another Availability Zone in the same Region.
options.note: Multi-Attach works only with Provisioned IOPS volumes and only for instances in the same Availability Zone as the volume. It cannot attach a volume across Availability Zones.

options.text: Attach a second gp3 volume to the instance and mirror the two volumes in a RAID 1 array so that either volume can fail without data loss.
options.note: Both volumes are in the same Availability Zone as the instance. An Availability Zone failure would make both volumes unavailable.

options.text: Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to continuously replicate the instance to a staging area in another Availability Zone.
options.note: Elastic Disaster Recovery would meet the requirements with an RPO of seconds, but its continuous replication costs more than the 4-hour RPO and 8-hour RTO require.

explanation: EBS volumes live in one Availability Zone, but their snapshots are stored regionally and can be restored in any Availability Zone. Scheduled snapshots are the cheapest way to meet an RPO and RTO measured in hours.

A company runs a containerized web service on a single Amazon EC2 instance that runs Docker. The service keeps WebSocket connections open to clients for several hours. The instance failed last week and the service was down until an engineer launched a new instance.

The company wants the service to remain available if an Availability Zone fails. The company does not want to manage servers or operating systems.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon ECS service on Amazon EC2 container instances in an Auto Scaling group that spans three Availability Zones. Run three tasks behind an Application Load Balancer.
options.note: This is highly available, but the company must manage the EC2 container instances and their operating systems.

options.text: Create an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate with all three tasks in a single subnet behind an Application Load Balancer.
options.note: Fargate removes server management, but one subnet is in one Availability Zone. All tasks would stop if that Availability Zone failed.

options.text: Create an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate with subnets in three Availability Zones and a desired count of three tasks behind an Application Load Balancer.
options.note: Amazon ECS spreads the service's tasks across the Availability Zones of the configured subnets and replaces failed tasks. Fargate removes the need to manage servers.

options.text: Package the service as an AWS Lambda container image. Invoke it through an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API.
options.note: API Gateway WebSocket APIs with Lambda are serverless and span Availability Zones, but an API Gateway WebSocket connection can stay open for at most 2 hours. Connections that must stay open for several hours would be dropped, and the service would need to be rewritten as Lambda handlers.

explanation: An ECS service on Fargate with subnets in multiple Availability Zones provides Availability Zone-level resilience without server management. The same service in one subnet, or on self-managed EC2 instances, each breaks one requirement.

A company runs an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster that has a single writer instance and no Aurora Replicas. When the writer instance failed recently, the database was unavailable for about 10 minutes while Aurora created a new instance.

The company wants to reduce database downtime when the writer instance or its Availability Zone fails.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an RDS Proxy for the DB cluster and configure the application to connect through the proxy.
options.note: RDS Proxy shortens client-side failover disruption, but there is still no replica to promote. Aurora must still create a new writer instance, so most of the downtime remains.

options.text: Add an Aurora Replica to the DB cluster in a different Availability Zone from the writer instance.
options.note: When an Aurora Replica exists, Aurora promotes it to writer during a failover, which is much faster than creating a new instance. Placing it in a different Availability Zone also covers an Availability Zone failure.

options.text: Enable Aurora Backtrack on the DB cluster with a target backtrack window of 24 hours.
options.note: Backtrack rewinds the database to an earlier point in time to undo logical errors. It does not provide a standby instance for failover.

options.text: Modify the writer instance to a larger instance class so that a replacement instance starts faster.
options.note: The instance class does not meaningfully change how long Aurora takes to create and start a replacement instance. Without a replica, failover still requires creating a new instance.

explanation: Aurora storage is already replicated across three Availability Zones, but compute is not: without an Aurora Replica, recovery means creating a new instance. Adding a replica in another Availability Zone gives Aurora a ready target to promote.

A company runs 40 Amazon EC2 instances in the us-east-1 Region. The instances host stateful applications, including several self-managed databases, that store data on Amazon EBS volumes. The company needs a DR solution in the us-east-2 Region.

The DR plan requires an RPO of seconds and an RTO of minutes. The company wants to keep standby costs low and cannot change the applications.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS Backup plan that backs up the instances every hour and copies each recovery point to us-east-2. Restore the instances during a disaster.
options.note: Hourly backups can lose up to an hour of data, and restoring 40 instances from backups takes longer than minutes.

options.text: Create an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy that snapshots the EBS volumes every hour and copies the snapshots to us-east-2.
options.note: Hourly snapshots cannot meet an RPO of seconds, and the instances would still need to be rebuilt from the snapshots during a disaster.

options.text: Run a full-size copy of each instance in us-east-2. Configure application-level replication between each pair of instances.
options.note: Full-size standby instances increase standby costs, and adding application-level replication requires changes that the company cannot make.

options.text: Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to replicate the instances continuously to a staging area in us-east-2. Launch recovery instances in a disaster.
options.note: Elastic Disaster Recovery supports cross-Region replication of EC2 instances. Continuous block-level replication gives an RPO of seconds, recovery instances launch in minutes, and only a low-cost staging area runs before a disaster.

explanation: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery works for EC2 instances between Regions as well as for on-premises servers. It replicates at the block level without application changes and keeps standby costs low, while backups and snapshots cannot reach a seconds-level RPO.

A company runs an application in the us-east-1 and us-west-2 Regions that reads and writes objects in Amazon S3. The company wants the application in both Regions to use a single global S3 endpoint. Normally all requests must go to a bucket in us-east-1. If S3 in us-east-1 has problems, the company wants to shift all requests to a bucket in us-west-2 within minutes. Objects written to either bucket must be available in the other bucket.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Create an S3 Multi-Region Access Point that contains both buckets. Use failover controls to set the us-east-1 bucket as active and the us-west-2 bucket as passive.
options.note: A Multi-Region Access Point gives one global endpoint. Its failover controls route all requests to the active bucket and can shift traffic to the passive bucket within minutes.

options.text: Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication rules in both directions between the two buckets.
options.note: Two-way replication keeps both buckets in sync, so objects written to either bucket, including writes made after a failover, are available in the other.

options.text: Configure an S3 Cross-Region Replication rule from the us-east-1 bucket to the us-west-2 bucket only.
options.note: One-way replication copies objects only from us-east-1. Objects written to the us-west-2 bucket after a failover would not be copied back.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the us-east-1 bucket and configure the application to use the accelerated endpoint.
options.note: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers to one bucket. It provides no failover to a bucket in another Region.

options.text: Create Amazon Route 53 failover records that point to the static website endpoints of the two buckets.
options.note: S3 static website endpoints support only read requests over HTTP. The application could not write objects through them.

explanation: S3 Multi-Region Access Points provide a single global endpoint, and failover controls give active-passive routing between buckets. Pair them with two-way replication so that the buckets stay in sync no matter which one is active.

text:
A company runs a document processing application on Amazon EC2 instances that share an Amazon EFS file system in the eu-west-1 Region. The company needs a copy of the file system in the eu-central-1 Region for DR.

The DR plan requires an RPO of 30 minutes. The company wants the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure Amazon EFS replication from the file system to a destination file system in eu-central-1.
options.note: EFS replication keeps a read-only copy of the file system in another Region and is designed for an RPO of about 15 minutes for most file systems. It is a managed setting with no scheduling to maintain.

options.text: Create an AWS DataSync task that copies the file system to a file system in eu-central-1. Schedule the task to run every hour.
options.note: DataSync can copy between EFS file systems, but an hourly schedule cannot meet a 30-minute RPO, and the company must manage the task.

options.text: Create an AWS Backup plan that backs up the file system every hour and copies each backup to eu-central-1.
options.note: Hourly backups plus the copy time give an RPO of more than an hour, which misses the 30-minute RPO.

options.text: Change the file system to use the EFS Regional storage classes with mount targets in every Availability Zone in eu-west-1.
options.note: Regional storage protects against the loss of an Availability Zone. It does not keep a copy of the data in eu-central-1.

explanation: EFS replication is the managed way to keep an EFS file system copied to another Region with an RPO of minutes. Scheduled copies and backups are bounded by their schedule and need more management.

A gaming company stores live leaderboards in an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster with Multi-AZ enabled in the us-east-1 Region. The leaderboard data exists only in the cache, and rebuilding it from game logs takes several hours.

The company needs a DR plan for a Regional outage with an RPO of seconds and an RTO of minutes. The solution must require the LEAST operational overhead.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Schedule daily ElastiCache backups, export them to Amazon S3, and copy them to the us-west-2 Region. Restore a new cluster from the latest backup during a disaster.
options.note: Daily backups can lose up to a day of data, and creating a new cluster from a backup takes longer than minutes.

options.text: Change the application to write every update to the existing cluster and to a second ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster in the us-west-2 Region.
options.note: Dual writes could meet the RPO, but the company must build and maintain the logic to keep both clusters consistent when writes fail. This adds operational overhead.

options.text: Create an ElastiCache (Redis OSS) Global Datastore with the existing cluster as the primary and a secondary cluster in the us-west-2 Region. Promote the secondary cluster during a disaster.
options.note: Global Datastore provides fully managed cross-Region replication, typically with less than 1 second of lag. The secondary cluster can be promoted to primary in minutes or less.

options.text: Add replicas to the existing cluster in all Availability Zones in us-east-1 and enable automatic failover.
options.note: More replicas improve resilience to node and Availability Zone failures, but all of them are in us-east-1. They do not protect against a Regional outage.

explanation: ElastiCache Global Datastore is the managed cross-Region replication feature for Redis OSS, giving an RPO of about a second and fast promotion. Multi-AZ replicas handle Availability Zone failures only, and backups cannot meet a seconds-level RPO.

A company uses Amazon Route 53 failover routing for a web application. The primary alias record points to an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in the us-east-1 Region with Evaluate Target Health enabled. The secondary record points to a standby environment in the us-west-2 Region. The ALB target group health check requests the path /, which returns a static page.

Last week the application's database in us-east-1 failed. Users received errors for an hour, but Route 53 did not fail over. The company wants Route 53 to fail over whenever the application in us-east-1 cannot process requests, including when a dependency such as the database fails.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Reduce the TTL of the failover records to 10 seconds so that clients receive the secondary record sooner.
options.note: A shorter TTL speeds up failover once Route 53 decides the primary is unhealthy. It does not change how health is detected, so Route 53 would still not fail over.

options.text: Add a /health path to the application that tests its database connection. Create a Route 53 health check that requests /health through the ALB and associate it with the primary record.
options.note: A health check that exercises the application's dependencies fails when the database is unavailable. Route 53 then treats the primary record as unhealthy and answers with the secondary record.

options.text: Create a Route 53 health check that requests the path / through the ALB and associate it with the primary record.
options.note: The / path returns a static page that does not touch the database. The health check would keep passing during a database failure.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the ALB's HealthyHostCount metric. Create a Route 53 health check that monitors the alarm and associate it with the primary record.
options.note: The targets keep passing the ALB's / health check during a database failure, so HealthyHostCount stays normal and the alarm never fires.

explanation: DNS failover is only as good as the health signal behind it. A shallow health check on a static page cannot detect dependency failures; a health check against an endpoint that exercises the critical dependencies makes Route 53 fail over when the application cannot actually serve requests.
